title: 観世流謡本 (Kanze-ryū Utaibon), Vol. 11a
shelf_note: Woodblock-printed Kanze-school chant books (utaibon) with red annotations by a later owner. The sampled pages are Tsunemasa, Kochō and Torioibune. This is Japanese literary tradition.
structure_note: There are 152 page records with OCR, but pages_count is 102 and pages_translated is 96. Images carry 'sp' ids, so the leaves look split after the counts were set: the count fields are stale, not a missing-page problem. Only 5 printed numbers were read. The 2 backsteps and 1 repeat are most likely misread folio numerals in the margin, not a broken order.

book_verdict: The NDL-koten transcription follows the printed utai text fairly well, but it reads chant notation as numerals and once invents a full date. The English on all four pages is unrelated or invented verse.
reader_summary: An 1840s Kanze-school chant book holding several Noh plays (Tsunemasa, Kochō, Torioibune). The transcription is mostly of the right text, with notation junk and one invented date. The English cannot be trusted: on every sampled page it invents imagery and drops the allusions and plot.

title: 観世流謡本 (Kanze-ryū Utaibon), Vol. 3
shelf_note: Kanze chant books. The sampled pages are from Yorimasa (Byōdō-in, the fan-shaped lawn), Hachi-no-ki and Hagoromo. Japanese Noh tradition.
structure_note: There are 167 page records with OCR, but pages_count is 112 and pages_translated is 108: stale count fields after a split ('sp' image ids). The 4 backsteps and 4 repeats among only 9 read printed numbers are most likely misread margin folios. The volume binds several plays, so a change of play between pages is expected, not a splice.

tr_errors.problem: Sense reversed. The source says he will put on the armour though it is torn, carry the halberd though it is rusty, and ride the horse though it is thin. The English has him discard the gear and the man grow thin.

book_verdict: The transcription is mostly sound. Its repeated defect is a margin play title read as an invented date ('十一月十一日'). The English is unusable: it renames Byōdō-in, reverses Tsuneyo's vow in Hachi-no-ki, and invents most lines.
reader_summary: A 19th-century Kanze chant book binding several plays (Yorimasa, Hachi-no-ki, Hagoromo). The Japanese transcription is close to the printed text apart from invented date headers. The English does not follow the source and cannot be used, even for the gist.

title: 観世流改訂謡本 (Kanze-ryū Noh Texts)
shelf_note: A 1912 revised Kanze chant book of Tamura. It fits the Japanese shelf. The 'americana' collection tag is wrong (it comes from the UIUC scan source).
structure_note: 28 records, all with OCR, 25 translated, and the counts agree. Page 3 is the opening leaf, half covered by a pasted UIUC library due-date slip. The 1 backstep and 1 repeat are likely misread folios. The OCR self-tags the pages 'handwritten', but this is a printed cursive (typeset/lithographed) utaibon.

book_verdict: A clean 1912 printed Tamura. The OCR substitutes text on the shimai page, misreads Washio-dera despite the printed ruby, and interleaves notation as glosses. The translations follow those errors.
reader_summary: The Noh play Tamura in a 1912 revised Kanze chant book. The transcription is of the right play but substitutes whole lines on at least one page and garbles names. The English is a rough paraphrase at best and cannot be trusted for temple names or the dance-song.

title: Genji Monogatari Ekotoba (源氏物語絵詞), Vol. 1
shelf_note: An NDL handscroll of Genji illustrations with calligraphy panels (NDL label: 源氏物語絵巻, call no. ん-98). The sampled text is from Yadorigi and Azumaya. Core Japanese literature.
structure_note: 19 scroll segments, counts consistent. Metadata published='1100' is wrong for this object: it is a later copy (the NDL acquisition stamps are Meiji 44 and Taishō 1), not the 12th-century scroll. The title 'Ekotoba' differs from the NDL's own title 絵巻.

book_verdict: A handsome illustrated Genji scroll, and the NDL-koten transcription of its calligraphy is largely usable. The English is fabricated on every text page, the catalogue date of 1100 is wrong, and one note dismisses the Genji text as 'tropes'.
reader_summary: A later copy of an illustrated Genji handscroll from the National Diet Library, with text panels from the Uji chapters (Yadorigi, Azumaya). The paintings and the Japanese transcription are worth opening. The English must not be relied on: it does not translate the panels, and it does not render the poems.
